land.text: the Median realm, from northeastern Iran to the Kızılırmak: 'in 550 BC succeeded in defeating the Medes'

predecessors.note: Persia itself, Cyrus' kingdom of Anshan (king since 559), is not a Cliopatria row.

land.text: the empire Alexander conquered in 334-330: Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia and, to 327, the east under Bessus

successors.note: Cliopatria books Egypt and the Levant of 331-327 to its Ptolemaic Kingdom row (1.22 M km2 in 331) and 4.7 M km2 of Iran and Central Asia to the Macedonian Empire only from 323.

capitals.name: Pasargadae
capitals.note: Infobox: 'Pasargadae (Cyrus the Great)'. The page gives no years for Cambyses; the end year is the researcher's reading of Darius' accession (522).

capitals.name: Susa
capitals.note: Infobox: 'Susa (Darius the Great)'; Darius' chancery sat at 'Persepolis, Susa, and Babylon'. Persepolis (lon 52.89, lat 29.94) was the 'ceremonial capital', Ecbatana and Babylon seats too; 'Artaxerxes moved the capital back to Persepolis' (undated). Years are the researcher's reading of an infobox without them.

capitals.name: Persepolis
capitals.note: The capital Alexander burned in 330 BC.

rulers.name: Cyrus the Great
rulers.note: Infobox 559-530 BC; king of Anshan from 559 and of the empire from 550.

rulers.name: Artaxerxes III
rulers.note: The Artaxerxes III page: accession 'sometime between November 359 and March 358 BC', death late August or late September 338.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 550 outline without the east and Susiana: the campaigns in the east ran 'between around 545 BC to 540 BC' and 'By the year 540 BC, Cyrus captured Elam and its capital, Susa' (Cyrus the Great); the Median realm that Cyrus took in 550 ran 'from northeastern Iran to the Kızılırmak River' (Medes). Lydia (546), the rest of Asia Minor (542), Elam and the east (540) and Babylonia (539) enter through the ledger

keyframe_review.note: 3.33 M km2 in the table (3.1 M by the gazetteer grid), against about 1.9 M km2 after the correction. The shape is Iran, all of Afghanistan, south Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, a corner of Pakistan and the Turkish half of Anatolia up to the Halys: that is the Median realm plus Persia plus the conquests the Cyrus page dates 545-540, so it draws 540 in 550. The infobox gives no area for 550 (5.5 M km2 is for about 500 BC); the Median dynasty infobox gives 2.8 M km2 for 585 BC. The correction is the state at its first year; the ledger carries the growth to Cliopatria's 540 outline.

3.71 M km2: Lydia, Ionia, Caria, Lycia, Cilicia (Turkey 92 percent), the east and Susiana are in, Babylonia (539) and Egypt are not. Harpagus 'ended in 542 BC' the conquest of Asia Minor and 'By the year 540 BC, Cyrus captured Elam and its capital, Susa' (Cyrus the Great). Babylon (October 539) is a ledger gain inside this interval, and Cliopatria's Neo-Babylonian shape runs to 531, so the two overlap there. No infobox area for 540.

4.27 M km2: Mesopotamia and the Levant are in (Cliopatria books them from 530, nine years after October 539), Egypt and Cyprus are not. The shape is right for its first year, 530, the year Cambyses became co-ruler ('In 530 BCE, his father made him co-ruler'); Cyprus and Egypt (525) and the Indus (515) are ledger gains inside the interval that Cliopatria draws only from 500. The page infobox area (5.5 M km2, c. 500 BC) is for the end state.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 500 outline plus Thrace, 'which had nominally been part of the Persian empire since 513 BC' (Greco-Persian Wars); Macedonia is a vassal, drawn by the ledger's vassal pair, not part of the shape

keyframe_review.note: 5.55 M km2 against the infobox's 'about 5,500,000 km2 around 500 BC' (ratio 1.01): the largest agreement in the dossier. The outline holds Egypt, Cyprus, the Indus (60 percent of Pakistan) and a strip of Libya; it lacks Thrace, nominally Persian since 513. Macedonia's submission (about 512-511) is a vassal event, not a shape. The Ionian Revolt (499-493) is a contest event.

5.62 M km2 (ratio 1.02 to the infobox): the high-water mark, with Thrace, parts of Macedonia and northern Greece (Greece 21 percent, Bulgaria 21 percent). Right for 480-479 only: 'In 480 BC, Xerxes initiated and personally led the second Persian invasion of Greece', and after Plataea (479), Sestos (479) and Byzantium (478) 'These consecutive losses would force Persian troops to eventually withdraw from Europe'. The ledger removes Europe in 479-478 and Ionia in 466 ('completely liberated Ionia' at the Eurymedon); Cliopatria's 450 shape shows the result.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 450 outline without Ionia: 'In 466 BC, the League achieved a double victory in the Battle of the Eurymedon, which completely liberated Ionia'; Persian control returned only with the King's Peace of 387 (Peace of Antalcidas page)

keyframe_review.note: 5.53 M km2 (ratio 1.00 to the infobox, c. 500 BC). Cliopatria keeps 65 percent of Ionia and 64 percent of Caria here; the page says Ionia was liberated in 466 and the 387 treaty's 'single greatest effect' was 'the return of firm Persian control over Ionia'. The Persian position in Ionia between 412 and 387 is not on the pages opened (a satrap at Sardis; Sparta's war) and is left to the gap-fillers. Peace of Callias (449): 'purported', no terms on the page.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 404 outline without Egypt and Cyrenaica: 'In 405 BC Amyrtaeus, with the help of Cretan mercenaries expelled the Persians from Memphis', and declared himself pharaoh the next year (404), 'ending the 27th Dynasty'; Ionia is still out until 387

keyframe_review.note: 4.99 M km2. Cliopatria drops Egypt only in 383 although the Persian satrapy ended in 404 ('a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire between 525 and 404 BC'); Artaxerxes II 'was still recognized as pharaoh in some parts of Egypt as late as 401 BC'. The outline also drops the Indus lands (Pakistan 59 to 10 percent) in 404 with no page behind it: kept at confidence 1 in the ledger. Cyprus stays in the shape; the Evagoras years (Cyprus outside Persian control about 391-381) are not on the pages opened.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 383 outline plus Cyprus: the King's Peace (387) decreed 'the cities in Asia should belong to him, as well as Clazomenae and Cyprus among the islands'; 'Ionia and Cyprus were abandoned to the Persians'

keyframe_review.note: 4.31 M km2. Cliopatria shows Egypt gone and Ionia back from 383 but no Cyprus until 366; the page puts Cyprus and Ionia under Persia from the 387 treaty. The pages do not say how much of Cyprus the king held in fact. No infobox area for this period.

4.32 M km2: the Cliopatria outline with Cyprus and Ionia and without Egypt. Artaxerxes III's page records the satrap revolts (Artabazus, 356) but no territorial change in 366-351; Egypt 'had revolted under his father, Artaxerxes II'.

4.33 M km2, Egypt out. 'In around 351 BC, Artaxerxes embarked on a campaign to recover Egypt' and failed; 'Soon after this Egyptian defeat, Phoenicia, Anatolia and Cyprus declared their independence'; the reconquest is dated 343 BC on the Achaemenid Empire page and the Twenty-seventh Dynasty page, 'probably 340 or 339' on the Artaxerxes III page. The outline is right for 350-344 (Egypt out); the Egyptian gain (343) is a ledger event and Cliopatria's next shape, with Egypt back, begins in 337.

5.01 M km2: Egypt, Cyprus and Libya back, Anatolia whole. Right from the reconquest, which the Achaemenid Empire page dates 343 BC ('In 343 BC, Artaxerxes III ... invaded Egypt'); Cliopatria starts it in 337, a few years after the 340/339 of the Artaxerxes III page. Darius III reigned 336-330; Alexander invaded in 334.

4.60 M km2: Anatolia west of the Halys gone (Turkey 45 percent), Egypt, Syria and the Levant still in. 'Alexander ... began his invasion of the Persian Empire in 334 BC' and won at Granicus and 'at the Battle of Issus in 333 BC' (Darius III). The Darius III and Achaemenid Empire pages do not mention Tyre, Gaza or Mazaces: the loss of the Levant and Egypt (332) is recorded at confidence 1/3 in the ledger (Egypt: 'That second period ended in 332 BC').

correction.text: the shape unchanged for 331 and 330 only: Gaugamela (331), Babylon, Susa and Persepolis taken (Persepolis burned in 330), Darius killed in July 330; Cliopatria's 327 end belongs to Alexander's empire. The ledger removes Mesopotamia and Susiana (331), Persis and Media (330) and ends the state in July 330

keyframe_review.note: 3.51 M km2 (Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia, Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia): Darius's rump before Gaugamela, then the east under Darius and Bessus. The Achaemenid infobox says 'Fall to Macedonia: 330 BC' and the Darius III page 'Died: July 330 BC'; Cliopatria runs this shape to 327. Bessus 'took the regal name Artaxerxes V' in the east; the 330-327 remnant is not on the pages beyond that sentence. No infobox area for this period.

region.text: Persia, Cyrus' kingdom of Anshan

ledger.note: 550: Cyrus the Great founds the Achaemenid Empire by defeating the Medes. Infobox 'founded by Cyrus the Great' in 550 BC; 'in 550 BC succeeded in defeating the Medes'. Cyrus had been king of Anshan since 559 and a Median vassal (Cyrus the Great, Medes pages).

region.text: the Median realm taken from Astyages, from northeastern Iran to the Kızılırmak (Halys)

ledger.note: 550: the Median realm passes to Cyrus. 'in 550 BC succeeded in defeating the Medes' and took Ecbatana; the Medes page: 'a territory stretching roughly from northeastern Iran to the Kızılırmak River in Anatolia' (drawn as the Median dossier's corrected outline).

region.text: the Lydian kingdom, Sardis its capital

ledger.note: 546: Cyrus conquers Lydia. 'Cyrus occupied the capital at Sardis, conquering the Lydian kingdom in 546 BC' (the page: 'The exact dates of the Lydian conquest are unknown'; the Achaemenid Empire infobox says 547).

region.text: Commagene

ledger.note: 546: 'Commagene was incorporated into Persia in 546 BC.' The page names no previous ruler.

region.text: Ionia, Caria and Lycia, the last of Asia Minor

ledger.note: 542: Harpagus completes the conquest of Asia Minor. 'Cyrus then sent Harpagus to finish the conquest of Asia Minor, which Harpagus ended in 542 BC'; Harpagus took Lycia, Aeolia and Caria and Mazares had subdued Magnesia and Priene. The page does not say that Ionia was taken as a whole.

region.text: Cilicia

ledger.note: Page silent: the Cyrus the Great page does not mention Cilicia, but Cliopatria's 540 outline holds it (87 percent) and the page has Harpagus 'finish the conquest of Asia Minor' in 542.

region.text: Elam and its capital Susa (Susiana)

ledger.note: 540: Cyrus takes Elam and Susa. 'By the year 540 BC, Cyrus captured Elam and its capital, Susa.' The page gives 'by', not an exact year; the region is Susiana (Khuzestan), the part of Elam not already Persia's core.

region.text: Bactria, Arachosia, Sogdia, Saka and Chorasmian lands, Margiana: the eastern provinces of Cyrus' campaigns

ledger.note: 540: Cyrus' eastern campaigns end. Cyrus attacked Bactria, Arachosia, Sogdia, Saka, Chorasmia, Margiana and other eastern provinces in campaigns 'between around 545 BC to 540 BC' (Sogdia 'during his military campaigns of 546-539 BC'); 'In 533 BC, Cyrus the Great crossed the Hindu Kush mountains and collected tribute from the Indus cities'. Placed at the end of the span, which is where Cliopatria's outline takes the east; the page names peoples, not states.

region.text: the Phoenician city-states of the Levant coast

ledger.note: Page undated: 'By 525 BC, Cambyses had successfully subjugated Phoenicia and Cyprus', and the Phoenician fleet made up 'a large part of Cambyses' fleet'. Dated to the fall of Babylon because Cliopatria's Babylonian outline holds the coast (Phoenicia 82 percent) and the Phoenicia dossier ends the Phoenician city-states under Persia in 539.

region.text: Babylonia and its dependencies, Babylon taken in October

ledger.note: 539: Cyrus takes Babylon. 'Just before October 539 BC, Cyrus fought the Battle of Opis' and 'entered the city of Babylon'; Nabonidus surrendered. The Syria-Palestine of the Babylonian outline came with it (Cyrus 'probably incorporated' Syria, Judea and Arabia Petraea, 'although there is no direct evidence to support this assumption'). Cliopatria keeps the Neo-Babylonian shape to 531 and gives the land to the Achaemenid outline only from 530.

region.text: Cyprus, seized from Amasis II before the Egyptian campaign

ledger.note: 525 or before: Cyprus passes to Persia. 'Cambyses, before starting his expedition into Egypt, had seized Cyprus from Amasis II'; the Achaemenid Empire page: 'By 525 BC, Cambyses had successfully subjugated Phoenicia and Cyprus'. The Twenty-sixth Dynasty dossier dates the passing of Cyprus to Persia at 545 from its own page ('Egyptian rule lasted for about 25 years until 545 BC'); the Cambyses II page dates it only as before the Egyptian campaign.

region.text: Cyrene and Barca

ledger.note: 525: 'In 525 BC, after conquering Egypt, the Achaemenid (Persian) army of Cambyses II seized the Pentapolis' (Cyrenaica page). The Cambyses II page: 'The Libyans, and soon the Greeks of Cyrene and Barca, willingly acknowledged the authority of Cambyses'; Achaemenid Empire page: 'surrendered to Cambyses and sent tribute without a fight'. Cliopatria's 500 outline holds a strip of Libya. Reviewer me-05-a: year from the Cyrenaica page (confidence 1 to 2); the greek-city-states dossier books the same event as a loss of Cyrenaica to this state.

region.text: Egypt, the Nile Valley and Delta, taken after Pelusium

ledger.note: 525: Cambyses II conquers Egypt. Psamtik III 'was defeated by Cambyses II at the Battle of Pelusium in the eastern Nile Delta in May of 525'; Egypt is 'a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire between 525 and 404 BC'. Cliopatria keeps its Twenty-sixth Dynasty shape to 501.

region.text: the lands surrounding the Indus River, from Gandhara to modern Karachi

ledger.note: 515: Darius I conquers the Indus. 'Darius conquered the lands surrounding the Indus River in 515 BCE' after wintering 516-515 in Gandhara; the page describes control 'from Gandhara to modern Karachi'. Drawn as the Pakistani part of Cliopatria's 500 outline.

region.text: Thrace

ledger.note: 513: Thrace becomes Persian. Thrace 'had nominally been part of the Persian empire since 513 BC' (Darius also 'invaded European Scythia in 513 BCE' and 'was repulsed from Scythia in 513', Achaemenid Empire page). The word 'nominally' makes the extent soft.

region.text: Macedonia under Amyntas I

ledger.note: 512: Macedonia submits. 'The Macedonian king Amyntas I surrendered his country to the Persians in about 512-511'; Darius page: 'Macedonia submitted voluntarily, after the demand of earth and water, becoming a vassal kingdom'; Mardonius in 492 made it a 'fully subordinate client kingdom' (Greco-Persian Wars).

region.text: the Greek cities of Ionia

ledger.note: 499: the Ionian Revolt begins. 'lasting from 499 to 493 BC'; 'By 494 BC the Persian army and navy had regrouped'. The page does not name the zone beyond 'Asia Minor'.

region.text: the Greek cities of Ionia

ledger.note: 493: the Ionian Revolt ends in Persian victory ('lasting from 499 to 493 BC').

region.text: Attica, central Greece and Thessaly, 'most of Greece'

ledger.note: 480: Xerxes invades Greece. 'In 480 BC, Xerxes initiated and personally led the second Persian invasion of Greece'; Thermopylae 'allowed the Persian army to raze an evacuated Athens'; 'The Persians had now captured most of Greece.' The zone is the researcher's reading of 'most of Greece'.

region.text: Attica, central Greece and Thessaly, the land the Persians held after the invasion

ledger.note: 479: the Persians are driven from Greece. The Greeks 'decisively routed the Persian army in the Battle of Plataea' (479) and destroyed the fleet at Mycale.

region.text: Sestos on the Hellespont

ledger.note: 479: Sestos falls to the Greeks. The League 'expelling Persian garrisons from Sestos in 479 BC'.

region.text: Macedonia

ledger.note: Page gives the cause, not the year: the withdrawal from Europe after Sestos (479) and Byzantium (478) was 'allowing Macedonia and the Ionian cities to reassert independence'. Set at 479, the first of the two losses; the Macedonian Empire dossier (eu-02) also ends the vassalage in 479.

region.text: Byzantium

ledger.note: 478: Byzantium is lost. The League drove the Persians 'from Byzantium in 478 BC'.

region.text: Thrace, the Persian holdings in Europe

ledger.note: 478: the Persians leave Europe. 'These consecutive losses would force Persian troops to eventually withdraw from Europe', which the page gives no separate date for each holding; set at 478, the last of the two dated losses.

region.text: Ionia, 'completely liberated' at the Eurymedon

ledger.note: 466: the Eurymedon liberates Ionia. 'In 466 BC, the League achieved a double victory in the Battle of the Eurymedon, which completely liberated Ionia' (the Achaemenid Empire page gives 469 or 466).

region.text: the Delta and Memphis, taken by Inaros

ledger.note: 460: Inaros II rebels in Egypt. 'In 460 BC another major Egyptian rebellion took place, led by a Libyan chief named' Inaros II, with substantial Athenian help; Inaros briefly controlled large parts of Egypt and took Memphis.

region.text: the Delta and Memphis, held by Inaros

ledger.note: 454: the revolt is crushed. 'Inaros and his Athenian allies were finally defeated by a Persian army led by general Megabyzus in 454 BC.'

region.text: Memphis and the Delta, where Amyrtaeus' rebellion took ground

ledger.note: 405: Amyrtaeus drives the Persians out of Memphis. 'In 405 BC Amyrtaeus, with the help of Cretan mercenaries expelled the Persians from Memphis'; the page says the rebellion began 'potentially... as early as 411 BC'. The zone is the researcher's reading; the Twenty-eighth Dynasty dossier opens its contest in 405 too.

region.text: the Delta, where Amyrtaeus' rebellion began

ledger.note: 404: the rebellion succeeds. 'In 405 BC Amyrtaeus, with the help of Cretan mercenaries expelled the Persians from Memphis'; he declared himself pharaoh the next year.

region.text: Egypt, the Persian satrapy of Mudraya, lost to Amyrtaeus

ledger.note: 404: Egypt is lost. The 27th Dynasty was 'disestablished upon the rebellion and crowning of Amyrtaeus as Pharaoh'; Egypt had been 'a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire between 525 and 404 BC'. Three native dynasties (28th, 29th, 30th) then ruled it.

region.text: Cyrene and Barca

ledger.note: Page silent on the end of the Cyrenaican allegiance; set with the loss of Egypt, to which Libya went in Cliopatria's 383 Thirtieth Dynasty shape.

region.text: the Indus lands Cliopatria drops from 404

ledger.note: Page silent: no page opened dates the loss of the Indus. Cliopatria's outline falls from 59 to 10 percent of Pakistan in 404; recorded to explain the shape, to be checked.

region.text: the Greek cities of Asia, Clazomenae and Cyprus

ledger.note: 387: the King's Peace. 'the cities in Asia should belong to him, as well as Clazomenae and Cyprus among the islands'; 'The single greatest effect of the Peace was the return of firm Persian control over Ionia and parts of the Aegean' (the page: 'The King's Peace (387 BC)').

region.text: Phoenicia and Cyprus

ledger.note: Page undated: 'Soon after this Egyptian defeat [about 351], Phoenicia, Anatolia and Cyprus declared their independence from Persian rule'; Tennes, king of Sidon, defeated two satraps. Set a year after 351.

region.text: Phoenicia and Cyprus, the rebels' ground

ledger.note: 343: the Cyprian rebels are put down. 'In 343 BC, Artaxerxes committed responsibility for the suppression of the Cyprian rebels to Idrieus' and Idrieus 'succeeded in reducing Cyprus'; Tennes was put to death. The Achaemenid Empire page has Sidon burnt before the Egyptian campaign.

region.text: Egypt and the Libyan coast of the Thirtieth Dynasty's outline

ledger.note: 343: Artaxerxes III reconquers Egypt. 'In 343 BC, Artaxerxes III ... invaded Egypt' (infobox: reconquest of Egypt 343 BC), beginning a second Achaemenid period that 'ended in 332 BC' (Twenty-seventh Dynasty page). The Artaxerxes III page has 'probably in 340 or 339 BC'; Cliopatria starts the shape in 337.

region.text: western Anatolia, the satrapies Alexander entered after Granicus

ledger.note: 334: Alexander invades. 'began his invasion of the Persian Empire' in 334 BC, 'followed almost immediately by the victory of Alexander over the Persians at' the Granicus. The zone is the researcher's reading, the western Anatolia that Cliopatria's 333 outline loses.

region.text: western Anatolia, the satrapies Alexander entered after Granicus

ledger.note: Page thin: Alexander 'defeated the Persian armies at Granicus (334 BC)' and Issus (333 BC), but neither page says which satrapies fell when; the region is Cliopatria's 337 outline minus its 333 outline. Cliopatria's Macedonian Empire gets the same land in 333 (585,000 km2, Turkey).

region.text: western Anatolia, the satrapies Alexander entered after Granicus

ledger.note: Page silent on the end of fighting in Anatolia; set with Issus ('at the Battle of Issus in 333 BC').

region.text: Egypt, where the second Persian period ended

ledger.note: 332: Egypt falls to Alexander. The second Achaemenid period in Egypt 'ended in 332 BC'; the Darius III infobox gives 'Reign: 336-332 BC' as Pharaoh. Cliopatria books Egypt to its Ptolemaic row from 331.

region.text: Syria, Phoenicia and Palestine with the Cilician coast

ledger.note: Page silent: neither the Achaemenid Empire nor the Darius III page mentions Tyre or Gaza. Cliopatria's 331 outline has lost Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Cilicia; recorded at 332 to explain the shape.

region.text: Babylonia and Susiana

ledger.note: 331: Gaugamela. 'The Battle of Gaugamela, in which Alexander the Great defeated Darius III of Persia in 331 BC'; 'Alexander took possession of Babylon, Susa, and the Persian capital at Persepolis.' The page gives no year for Babylon or Susa.

region.text: Persepolis

ledger.note: 330: Persepolis burns. Alexander loots and destroys 'their capital, Persepolis, by fire in 330 BC'.

region.text: Ecbatana

ledger.note: Page silent on who held Ecbatana: Darius 'fled to Ecbatana and attempted to raise a third army', then 'decided to retreat to Bactria'. The zone passes to Alexander in the pursuit of 330.

region.text: Bactria and the east, where Bessus took the title of king

ledger.note: 330: Bessus claims the east. Darius 'was killed by his relative Bessus', who 'took the regal name Artaxerxes V and began calling himself the King of Asia'. The page gives no territory.

region.text: the whole empire as Cliopatria draws it in 331

ledger.note: 330: Darius III is killed and the empire ends. Infobox 'Died: July 330 BC'; Achaemenid Empire infobox 'Fall to Macedonia: 330 BC'. The land passes to Alexander (macedonian-empire); Bessus' remnant is not on the pages beyond one sentence.

wars.name: Revolts against Darius I
wars.outcome: All suppressed within a year: 'By 522 BCE, there were revolts against Darius in most parts of the Achaemenid Empire' and 'Darius was able to suppress and quell all revolts within a year.' No border moved.

wars.name: Cyrus' conquest of Lydia
wars.outcome: Persian victory at Thymbra and Sardis; the Lydian kingdom annexed in 546 BC (infobox 547). Harpagus finished Asia Minor in 542.
wars.note: 'The exact dates of the Lydian conquest are unknown.'

wars.name: Cyrus' campaigns in Central Asia
wars.outcome: The eastern provinces were taken: the campaigns in the east ran 'between around 545 BC to 540 BC'; the page names peoples and provinces, not states.
wars.note: Cyrus crossed the Hindu Kush in 533 and collected tribute from the Indus cities; the Indus itself fell to Darius in 515.

wars.name: Persian conquest of Babylon
wars.outcome: Cyrus defeated the Babylonians at Opis and entered Babylon in October 539; Nabonidus surrendered.

wars.name: Persian conquest of Egypt
wars.outcome: Cambyses II won at Pelusium (May 525) and took Memphis; Egypt became a satrapy to 404.
wars.note: Cambyses' Nubian and Siwa expeditions 'ended in catastrophe' (Herodotus, as the Cambyses II page cites him); no border moved.

wars.name: Darius I's Scythian campaign
wars.outcome: The army 'was repulsed from Scythia in 513 BC'; Thrace became nominally Persian and Macedonia submitted (about 512-511).

wars.name: Ionian Revolt
wars.outcome: Persian victory; the revolt 'lasting from 499 to 493 BC' was crushed after the Persian army and navy regrouped in 494 (Lade).

wars.name: First Persian invasion of Greece
wars.outcome: Mardonius made Macedon a 'fully subordinate client kingdom of Persia' in 492; the Persians were defeated at Marathon in 490 and withdrew.
wars.note: Eretria and the Cyclades are not on the pages opened.

wars.name: Second Persian invasion of Greece
wars.outcome: Xerxes razed Athens and 'captured most of Greece', then lost at Salamis (480) and Plataea and Mycale (479) and withdrew.

wars.name: Greek counter-offensive and Peace of Callias
wars.outcome: Sestos (479), Byzantium (478), Ionia freed at the Eurymedon (466), Cyprus contested (478, 451), Egypt (460-454); closed by the 'purported' Peace of Callias of 449, whose terms the page does not give.

wars.name: Revolt of Inaros II
wars.outcome: Persian victory under Megabyzus in 454 BC; Athenian forces besieged for 18 months and wiped out.

wars.name: Egyptian revolt of Amyrtaeus
wars.outcome: Amyrtaeus expelled the Persians from Memphis in 405 and was crowned in 404: Egypt independent for about sixty years.

wars.name: King's Peace (Peace of Antalcidas)
wars.outcome: 'the cities in Asia should belong to him, as well as Clazomenae and Cyprus among the islands'; Ionia and Cyprus returned to the Persians.
wars.note: The page describes the treaty, not the Corinthian War that led to it.

wars.name: Artaxerxes III's reconquest of Egypt and the Phoenician and Cypriot revolt
wars.outcome: The attack of about 351 failed and Phoenicia and Cyprus rose; Idrieus reduced Cyprus in 343 and Egypt was reconquered in 343 (Achaemenid Empire page) or 340/339 (Artaxerxes III page).

wars.name: Wars of Alexander the Great against Persia
wars.outcome: Granicus (334), Issus (333), Gaugamela (331), Persepolis burned (330), Darius III killed in July 330 by Bessus, who took the name Artaxerxes V.
wars.note: Tyre, Gaza and Mazaces are not on the pages opened.

certainty.note: No page opened gives a boundary line; the satrapies are named but not mapped, the treaties (Callias 449, Antalcidas 387) name cities and islands, not frontiers. Every edge is approximate; Thrace after 513 and the Indus after 515 are the softest.

notes:
Pages opened: nine (Achaemenid Empire, Cyrus the Great, Cambyses II, Darius the Great, Greco-Persian Wars, Twenty-seventh Dynasty of Egypt, Artaxerxes III, Peace of Antalcidas, Darius III), the budget for 13 shapes; the Median dossier's Medes and Median dynasty pages were read for the 550 handover.
Policy: a keyframe verdict describes the shape in the first year of its Cliopatria interval; the ledger carries what changes inside the interval, so a renderer that applies the ledger to the keyframe never shows land before its gain. Corrections are written against the gazetteer's own cells (Cliopatria shape minus or plus named regions); areas quoted are the table's.
Cliopatria problems found: (1) the 550-541 outline already holds Afghanistan, Central Asia, Susiana and the whole Turkish half of Anatolia, which Cyrus took in 545-540 (Cyrus page); corrected. (2) Cliopatria draws the Egyptian satrapy to 384 although it ended in 404, and draws the Indus lands falling in 404 with no page behind it (ledger event at confidence 1). (3) Ionia is kept at 65 percent from 450; the Greco-Persian Wars page says it was liberated in 466 and that Persian control returned in 387; the Persian grip in 412-387 is not on the pages opened. (4) Cyprus is missing from the 383 shape (Persian by the 387 treaty). (5) The 331-327 shape runs three years past the empire's end (July 330) and is mostly Alexander's; Cliopatria's Macedonian Empire row at 331-327 is 218,000 km2 in Greece and its Ptolemaic Kingdom row at 331 is 1.22 M km2 of Egypt, Syria and Turkey, so Alexander's conquests of 333-331 are split between those rows in a way no page supports. (6) The Neo-Babylonian, Twenty-sixth Dynasty and Lydia rows run past their conquests (531, 501, 541) and overlap this state's shapes.
Disagreements: Lydia 546 (text) against 547 (infobox); the reconquest of Egypt 343 (Achaemenid Empire page and Twenty-seventh Dynasty page) against 'probably 340 or 339' (Artaxerxes III page); the Eurymedon 466 against 469 or 466 (Achaemenid Empire page); Xerxes 486-465 (infobox) against 485-465 (text).
Not settled: the Cilician and Commagene status before 546/540; the Persian grip on Ionia 412-387; the Cyprus of Evagoras; Phoenicia's submission (Achaemenid Empire page: 'By 525 BC, Cambyses had successfully subjugated Phoenicia and Cyprus', not dated beyond that); the satrapies as internal units (the pages give 'between 20 and 30' and no list; Darius created twenty); the eastern frontier on the Indus after 404; Thrace's actual extent after 493 and the Hellespontine garrisons after 479 (Doriscus, Eion not on the pages); Tyre and Gaza 332; the Bessus remnant 330-327.
Counterparts needing dossiers: the Phoenician and Cypriot rebels (about 350-343), Bessus' state (330-329), Cyrene and Barca as a Persian vassal (525-404; the Cyrenaica dossier is a Cliopatria row from 331 only). Cross-dossier points for the reviewer: the Twenty-seventh Dynasty dossier models the Persian satrapy of Egypt (525-404) as a dynasty under Achaemenid occupation, while this dossier draws Egypt as Achaemenid land from 525 and has no occupation pair: one of the two models must be chosen or Egypt is drawn twice; the Twenty-sixth Dynasty dossier dates the loss of Cyprus to 545, this one to 525; the Macedonian Empire dossier (eu-02) records gains from the Achaemenid Empire at 329-327 (Bactria, Sogdia), after this dossier's end in July 330, where the Bessus remnant is a split event. Region names used: all in regions.jsonl or places.jsonl; the Hellespont coordinate stands for Sestos, which the gazetteer lacks.
